title: The project sponsor
blurb: What the sponsor owns, provides and decides, and how to pick out the sponsor in any exam scenario.
question: Halfway through a new patient-booking system, costs are forecast to rise beyond what the project manager is allowed to approve. The operations director who secured the funding is asked whether the project should continue. Why is this her decision?

teach.body: APM describes the sponsor as the senior individual accountable for ensuring the work is governed effectively and delivers the objectives that meet the identified need. In plain English: the sponsor is the senior person who wants the change, secures the money for it and answers to the organisation for whether it was worth doing. Every project should have exactly one sponsor, so there is never any doubt about where accountability sits.

teach.caption: Four verbs to remember: the sponsor OWNS, PROVIDES, DECIDES and LEADS. None of them is day-to-day delivery.

teach.body: Being accountable means the buck stops with you: you answer for the result even when others do the work. The sponsor delegates the day-to-day management of the project to the project manager, within agreed limits called tolerances, and then supports, challenges and decides. A sponsor who starts managing tasks has stepped into the project manager's role; a sponsor who disappears leaves the project with nobody to make the big decisions.

teach.h: Scenario: the Riverside clinic booking system
teach.body: Priya, Director of Operations, sponsors a new online booking system. She owns the business case (fewer missed appointments), secured the budget and appointed Tom as project manager. Tom may absorb cost variances of up to £15,000 without asking. When a supplier price rise threatens £40,000, the problem breaches his tolerance, so Tom escalates it as an issue. Priya, chairing the project board, checks the business case is still viable and decides to fund the rise.

root.label: A problem threatens the plan
root.sub: the project manager assesses its impact

children.label: PM resolves it
children.sub: and reports it to the sponsor

teach.caption: Tolerances are the limits the sponsor delegates. Inside them the PM acts; beyond them the sponsor decides.

rows.label: Updating the risk register each week

teach.text: The exam disguises project manager tasks as sponsor tasks: writing the project management plan, creating the work or cost breakdown structure, managing day-to-day risks. The sponsor APPROVES the plan and OWNS the business case; the project manager WRITES the plan and RUNS the work.

items: Sponsor: the senior individual accountable for the project being governed well and meeting the identified need.
Owns the business case and is accountable for benefits realisation, often after the project closes.
Secures funding and resources, appoints and supports the project manager, and champions the project.
Usually chairs the governance board, approves the PMP and gate decisions, and resolves escalated issues.

summary: You can now state what the project sponsor is accountable for, list what the sponsor owns, provides, decides and leads, and separate sponsor tasks from project manager tasks. You can also explain why a problem beyond the project manager's tolerance becomes the sponsor's decision.

A.q: Which role is accountable for the realisation of the benefits set out in the business case?
A.why: The sponsor owns the business case and is accountable for realising the benefits it promises, often after the project has closed.

whyNot.0: The project manager is responsible for delivering the outputs, not accountable for the benefits.
whyNot.2: The product owner maximises the value of each iteration's work but does not own the business case benefits.
whyNot.3: A PMO supports projects with standards, reporting and assurance; it is not accountable for any project's benefits.

A.q: Complete the statement: the sponsor is the senior individual accountable for ensuring the work is governed effectively and that it…
options: follows the methods set by the PMO
completes every work package on time
meets its objectives and the need
A.why: The sponsor's accountability is that the work is governed effectively and delivers the objectives that meet the identified need: the reason the project exists.

whyNot.0: Following PMO methods is about consistency; the sponsor's accountability is for the project meeting its need.
whyNot.1: Staying within tolerance is what the project manager is responsible for during delivery.
whyNot.2: Completing work packages on time is a delivery matter for the project manager and team.

A.q:
Which TWO of the following are responsibilities of the project sponsor?
1) Securing funding and resources
2) Maintaining the risk register
3) Approving the project management plan
4) Assigning work packages to the team
A.why: Securing funding and resources (1) and approving the project management plan (3) are sponsor responsibilities.

whyNot.1: Maintaining the risk register (2) is a project manager task, so this pair is only half right.
whyNot.2: Both 2 and 4 are day-to-day project manager tasks.
whyNot.3: Assigning work packages (4) belongs to the project manager, so this pair is only half right.

B.q: A project manager forecasts that a supplier failure will push costs beyond the agreed tolerance. Who should decide how to resolve it?
B.why: A problem that breaches the project manager's delegated tolerance is an issue, and it is escalated to the sponsor to agree a resolution.

whyNot.0: The team carries out the work; it has no authority to approve spending beyond tolerance.
whyNot.1: The PMO can help analyse and report the problem but does not make the sponsor's decisions.
whyNot.3: The supplier caused the problem but cannot decide how the client's project responds to it.

B.q: Which of the following is NOT a responsibility of the project sponsor?
options: Securing the funding for the project
Allocating tasks to the team daily
B.why: Allocating daily tasks is day-to-day management, which the sponsor delegates to the project manager.

whyNot.0: Securing funding is a core sponsor responsibility.
whyNot.1: The sponsor appoints and supports the project manager.
whyNot.2: Championing the project at senior level is part of the sponsor's role.

B.q: Which project document does the sponsor own?
B.why: The sponsor owns the business case: the justification for the project, which the sponsor keeps valid throughout.

whyNot.1: The project manager writes, owns and maintains the project management plan; the sponsor approves it.
whyNot.2: The project manager maintains the risk register.
whyNot.3: On iterative work, the product owner owns and prioritises the product backlog.

C.q: Eight months after handover, a hospital asks whether its new e-rostering system has cut agency staffing costs as promised. Who is accountable for this outcome?
C.why: Benefits often arrive after closure. The sponsor remains accountable for benefits realisation long after the project manager and team have moved on.

whyNot.0: The project manager's responsibility ends with delivering and handing over the outputs.
whyNot.2: End users adopt the system, which enables the benefits, but they are not accountable for them.
whyNot.3: The delivery team built the outputs; it is not accountable for business benefits.

C.q: Which action best shows a sponsor championing the project?
options: Promoting it to other senior leaders
C.why: Championing means promoting and defending the project at senior level so it keeps support, priority and resources.

whyNot.1: Updating the schedule is a project manager task.
whyNot.2: Testing outputs is done by the team and by end users at acceptance.
whyNot.3: Defining work packages is planning work led by the project manager.

C.q: Why does the sponsor role need to be held by a senior individual?
options: To manage the team's daily task list
To write the detailed delivery schedule
To have authority to fund and decide
To carry out the specialist project work
C.why: The sponsor must be senior enough to secure funding and resources and to make decisions beyond the project manager's authority.

whyNot.0: Managing daily tasks is the project manager's role and needs no senior authority.
whyNot.1: The project manager produces the schedule.
whyNot.3: Specialist work is carried out by project team members.

reteach.title: The sponsor is the client paying for the house extension
reteach.question: You are paying for a kitchen extension and have hired a builder to run the job. Which of you is the sponsor, and which jobs stay with you?

blocks.body: You decided you need the space, you hold the budget and you will live with the result. The builder (the project manager) plans the job, organises trades and deals with daily problems. If a small hitch costs a few hundred pounds, the builder sorts it. If the ground needs extra foundations costing thousands, the builder comes to you, because only you can decide whether the extension is still worth it.

blocks.text: If an option describes doing the work or running it day to day, it is not the sponsor. If it describes justifying, funding, deciding or answering for benefits, it is.

explain.body: The sponsor is the single senior person accountable for the project being governed effectively and meeting the identified need. Others are responsible for parts of the work; the sponsor answers for the whole.

items.label: sponsor per project, so accountability is clear
enough to secure funds and make decisions

test.q: Which word best describes the sponsor's position on the project's overall success?
test.why: The sponsor is accountable: the person who answers for the project's success and its benefits.

whyNot.0: Consulted describes someone whose views are sought, not the person who answers for the result.
whyNot.1: Informed describes someone kept up to date, far short of the sponsor's role.
whyNot.3: The sponsor is closely involved and invested, not independent of the project.

explain.h: Owns the business case and benefits
explain.body: The sponsor owns the business case, keeps it valid as things change and is accountable for the benefits it promises. The project manager contributes estimates and plans, but ownership stays with the sponsor.

steps.label: Outputs
steps.sub: Delivered by the PM and team

test.q: Which pair of items does the sponsor own or answer for?
test.why: The sponsor owns the business case and is accountable for realising the benefits.

whyNot.0: The schedule and work packages are planned and managed by the project manager.
whyNot.1: The project manager maintains the risk and issue logs.
whyNot.2: On iterative work the product owner owns the backlog, and time boxes are managed by the delivery team.

explain.body: The sponsor secures the funding and resources, appoints and supports the project manager, and champions the project at senior level so it keeps priority and support across the organisation.

test.q: A project needs specialists from another department, whose director is refusing to release them. Who should use senior influence to secure them?
test.why: Securing resources and championing the project at senior level are sponsor responsibilities.

whyNot.1: A team member has no authority over another director's staff.
whyNot.2: End users use the outputs; they do not secure project resources.
whyNot.3: A supplier cannot release the client organisation's own staff.

explain.body: The sponsor usually chairs the governance board, approves the project management plan, takes or confirms decisions at decision gates and agrees how to resolve issues escalated beyond the project manager's tolerances.

test.q: At a decision gate, who takes or confirms the go or no-go decision?
test.why: Decisions at gates are taken by the sponsor or the governance board the sponsor chairs.

whyNot.0: The project manager prepares information for the gate but does not decide whether the project continues.
whyNot.2: The team delivers the work; gate decisions are a governance matter.
whyNot.3: The PMO may support the gate review with assurance, but it does not decide.
